1.title: Linux Basics: Navigation
1.desc: In this module, you will learn how to move around the Linux filesystem. You will master the commands used to identify your current location, list files, and enter different directories. These are the fundamental skills every security researcher needs to audit a system.

tasks.desc: Identify your current location by printing the absolute path of the working directory.
List the files and folders in your current location to see what is available.
Change your current directory to the 'Documents' folder.
List all entries, including hidden files that start with a dot (.) which often contain configurations.
Move back up one level to the parent directory.

2.title: File Operations
2.desc: This lesson focuses on managing data. You will learn how to create, move, rename, and delete files and directories. Mastering these commands allows you to organize your tools and exfiltrate data efficiently during a penetration test.

tasks.desc: Create a new empty file named 'evidence.txt' in your current directory.
Create a new directory named 'Loot' to store collected data.
Copy the 'evidence.txt' file into the 'Loot' directory.
Rename 'evidence.txt' to 'discovery.txt' to hide its original purpose.
Permanently remove the file from the system to leave no trace.

3.title: System Information
3.desc: Before performing an attack, you must understand the target environment. This module teaches you how to gather system specs, kernel versions, and hardware information to choose the correct exploit for the target's architecture.

tasks.desc: Print all system information including the kernel version and architecture.
Display the username of the current effective user ID.
Show the amount of available disk space on file systems in human-readable format.
Display the amount of free and used memory in the system in Megabytes.
Find out how long the system has been running and the current load average.

4.title: Network Reconnaissance
4.desc: Networking is the backbone of cybersecurity. You will learn to identify your network interface, test connectivity to remote hosts, and perform fast port scans to find entry points into a target network.

tasks.desc: Display all network interfaces and their assigned IP addresses.
Send 4 ICMP packets to a host to verify if it is reachable on the network.
Perform a fast scan of the top 100 most common ports on the target IP.
tasks.res:
PORT 22/tcp open  ssh
PORT 80/tcp open  http

tasks.desc: List all active listening ports on your own machine to check for backdoors.
Query DNS servers to find the IP address associated with a domain name.

5.title: Permission Management
5.desc: Linux security relies on permissions. In this module, you will learn to read permission strings (rwx) and modify them to secure files or grant yourself execution rights on scripts.

tasks.desc: List files with detailed attributes including permissions, owner, and size.
Add execution permissions to a file so it can be run as a program.
Restrict a file so only the owner can read, write, or execute it.
Attempt to change the file owner to root (expect a permission error).
tasks.res: chown: changing ownership of 'secret.txt': Operation not permitted

tasks.desc: Use administrative privileges (sudo) to force a change in file ownership.

6.title: Package Management
6.desc: Modern Linux systems use package managers to install and update software. You will learn how to synchronize repositories and manage the lifecycle of security tools on your system.

tasks.desc: Download the latest package information from the configured repositories.
List all software packages currently installed on the system.
Install the Ncat networking utility from the official repositories.
tasks.res: ncat is already the newest version (7.93+dfsg1-1).

tasks.desc: Search the repositories for any software related to 'nmap'.
Uninstall insecure legacy protocols like Telnet from your machine.

7.title: Process Control
7.desc: A hacker must monitor what is running on the system. This lesson covers viewing active processes, monitoring CPU/RAM usage in real-time, and terminating unresponsive or malicious programs.

tasks.desc: List every process currently running on the system with user and PID details.
tasks.res:
USER PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND
user 1234 0.5 1.2 python3 game.py

tasks.desc: Launch an interactive real-time monitor for system processes and resource usage.
tasks.res:
Tasks: 120 total, 1 running, 119 sleeping
%Cpu(s): 2.5 us, 1.0 sy

tasks.desc: Send a SIGKILL signal to immediately stop a process using its Process ID (PID).
Check for any processes you have running in the background of this terminal.
Resume a suspended job by running it in the background.

8.title: Credential Auditing
8.desc: This module introduces the basics of password security. You will learn how Linux stores user accounts and how to use specialized tools like Hydra and John the Ripper to audit credential strength.

tasks.desc: Read the file containing basic user account information (excluding passwords).
Perform a targeted SSH login test using the password '123'.
Use John the Ripper to crack password hashes using a wordlist.
Identify and list available hardware (CPU/GPU) for high-speed hash cracking.
View the encrypted password hash for the current user (requires root).

9.title: Exploitation Basics
9.desc: Metasploit is the industry-standard exploitation framework. In this lesson, you will learn to navigate the console, search for known vulnerabilities, and configure exploit parameters for a target.

tasks.desc: Launch the Metasploit Framework in quiet mode without the banner.
Search the Metasploit database for exploits targeting the EternalBlue vulnerability.
Select the first exploit from the search results to begin configuration.
List all required settings (IPs, Ports, Payloads) for the selected exploit.
tasks.res:
Name   Current Setting  Required
----   ---------------  --------
RHOSTS                  yes

tasks.desc: Terminate the Metasploit session and return to the standard Linux shell.

10.title: Persistence & Cleanup
10.desc: Ethical hackers must manage their footprint. This final module covers how persistence is established using scheduled tasks and the critical importance of cleaning up files and logs after a demo.

tasks.desc: List the scheduled jobs for the current user to find automated persistence scripts.
Audit the temporary directory for any installers or logs left behind.
Delete the temporary installer file to free up space and hide activity.
Run the custom RCA Cleanup tool to remove the crontab entry and hide the backdoor.
tasks.res: [*] Cleanup complete. System is now secure.

tasks.desc: Clear the bash command history so no one can see which commands were run.
